figures.caption: Figure 1: Design. (a) Two readers. A human participant reads text one word at a time while EEG is recorded. An LLM processes the same text one token at a time. Each token updates the LLM’s hidden states. We extract a hidden state from each layer of the LLM. Early layers represent token / word identity, whereas deeper layers are more contextual. Our EEG decoder learns to align a 0.5-s EEG window with the LLM’s hidden state for that word. We separately train one EEG decoder per layer (0–32), without and with a transformer over the sequence of EEG windows. (b) Lag-dependent run-mate swap. We have previously observed that our EEG decoder tracks the narrative context of text, and that this context tracking component is distinct from word-level decoding (Marquardt et al., 2026). Here, we conduct further tests on the context tracking. The lag-dependent run-mate swap probes how far the information shared between EEG trials reaches. Each trial’s own prediction is replaced by the prediction of a run-mate k trials earlier or later before computing the gain in retrieval accuracy over a permutation baseline. (c) Narrative neighbours across sessions. The context-tracking gain may be confounded by an EEG session signature that is unrelated to the text. To test this, we permute predictions within sessions and across sessions.

Figure 2: Word-level decodability across layers. (a) Within-run retrieval gain (candidates from the same passage; the primary metric) against the layer of Llama-3.1-8B the target embedding was taken from, for the decoder without a sequence model (orange) and with the transformer over EEG windows (blue). Lines and bands are the mean and SD over the five train/validation splits, and faint lines are the individual splits. (b) The same after subtracting the transformer’s position-only probe (without a sequence model (a) and (b) are identical because there is no positional embedding). Chance is 0 pp. The two decoders are indistinguishable at layer 0, where the target carries no context; word-level decodability peaks one or two blocks into the model and declines steadily with depth, and the shape is the same in every split. (b) shows that the profile survives removal of the transformer’s positional shortcut, indicating that the profile is the result of EEG-to-LLM alignment, and not a modelling confound.

Figure 3: Overall gain and its context-tracking share across layers. (a) Overall gain in random cross-run pools (where the correct word has to be selected among candidates from many different runs / text passages). (b) Its context-tracking component, measured by replacing every trial’s prediction with a randomly sampled prediction from the same run. (c) The context-independent remainder (overall minus context-tracking). (d) The context-tracking share of the overall gain. Conventions as in Figure 2. Panel (a) shows how much the decoder gains when candidates come from many passages, which is far more with the sequence model. (b) shows that the part of that gain earned by recognising the passage rises with depth for both decoders, i.e. also for the one without a sequence model that only sees a single EEG window (discussed in Section 3.5). (c) shows that the remaining context-independent gain (after subtracting the context-tracking component) follows the word-level metric’s slow decline towards the deep layers. (d) shows that the passage becomes a larger share of what the decoder reads with every layer.

Figure 4: Word-frequency bins across layers. Within-run gain for rare, mid-frequency and frequent words (tertiles by validation trial count, each against its own baseline) against layer, (a) without and (b) with the sequence model. (c) Rare-bin gain divided by frequent-bin gain; 1.0 would mean rare words decode as well as frequent ones. Means and SD over splits. Panels (a, b) show that frequent words drive the early peak, whereas rare and mid-frequency words keep improving further into the middle of the network; (c) makes the comparison directly: relative to frequent words, rare words are decoded worst against the context-free layer 0 and best against mid-depth targets.

Figure 5: Position probes and the transformer’s advantage across layers. (a) The transformer’s within-run gain decomposed into the position-only (non-neural), preceding-EEG and current-trial terms, per layer (means over splits; error bars are the SD of the within-run gain). (b) Transformer minus no-sequencemodel, paired within split, for the overall gain, the within-run gain and the position-corrected within-run gain. Panel (a) shows that the non-neural position-only term is flat across depth, so the depth profile of Figure 2 is explained by the EEG terms; (b) shows that the transformer’s advantage is large on the overall gain, where it is passage tracking, small on the position-corrected word-level metric, and slightly negative at layer 0, where the target carries no context for it to exploit.

Figure 6: Lag-dependent run-mate swap and the target-geometry control. (a, b) Cross-run gain after replacing each trial’s prediction with that of the run-mate |k| trials away (both directions averaged), for five layers, (a) without and (b) with the sequence model; dashed lines are the target-geometry control at the same layers. The profile shows how far along the run the information shared between trials reaches: a flat profile is a component that the whole run shares, a decaying one a local component, and the target-geometry control marks what word decoding with no context in the EEG would produce at each lag. Both without (a) and with (b) a sequence model, the profiles lie far above the control, so the decoder’s predictions share something that the geometry of the targets does not explain. Without a sequence model the profile is comparatively flat (note the different y-axis scales in (a) and (b)), so the shared component is run-level. With the sequence model the profile falls steeply with the lag of the swapped trial, so its context is local. (c, d) Against layer: the swap gain for a run-mate 4 and 256 trials away, the random-run-mate control of report 1, and the target-geometry control’s random swap. These panels show that the ordering of (a, b) holds at every layer, and that the run-level component grows with depth while the control stays at 1 pp or less without a sequence model and below 2 pp with it. Means and SD over splits.
Figure 7: Probing potential confounds that could explain the observed context-tracking gain.
